newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Italian banks on painfully slow road to reform.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Italian banks on painfully slow road to reform.

text.p: The mere mention of the word "bank' in Italy is enough to make most people see red.

The government accuses banks of not joining the fight against inflation, industrialists blame them for depressing the economy, investors charge them with inefficiency and clients say they're responsible for just about everything under the sun.

"There is no service culture with Italian banks and no shareholder-friendly culture. Most banks are overstaffed and many have major difficulties with bad debt," said Bryan Crossley, banking analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in London.
Banking chiefs have been trying for months to put their house in order but change has been painfully slow in a sector where 996 savings, regional and national banks jostle for trade.
At present only 37 banks are listed on the main Milan bourse and most of these are not fully floated.
This figure has prompted many people to argue that a rapid dose of privatisation is the key to solving the sector's problems. The trouble is, who wants to invest in the stock?

In a bid to boost share ownership, the 1994 government of Silvio Berlusconi ordered local, non-profit making foundations, which control a swathe of regional banks, to drop their holdings to under 50 percent by the end of 1998.

"This deadline will be postponed for sure," said an analyst at a top Milan brokerage. "One or two larger banks might do it but the vast majority stand no chance...There is no-one out there who wants to buy them," he added, declining to be named.

Investor reticence is understandable given the banks' recent performance on the Milan bourse, with banking stocks falling 10.61 percent since the start of 1993 while the general BCI bourse index rose 33.68 percent over the same period.

And bitterness still lingers over Italy's most recent stab at privatisations two years ago, when both Credito Italiano and Banca Commerciale Italiano fell firmly into the orbit of omnipotent merchant bank Mediobanca.
Within a year, both banks had unleashed hefty capital increases on their unwitting shareholders and their stocks are still languishing well below the original placement price.
"The capital increases and change of strategy were pretty shocking and still gall," said Sasha Serafimovski, banking analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The sector's image took another battering with the disclosure earlier this year of huge undisclosed bad debts at Banco di Napoli, which reported a 3.16 trillion lire ($2.1 billion) loss for 1995 -- the largest in Italy's banking history.
GOVERNMENT LEADING HUGE RECAPITALISATION PLAN
To keep Italy's premier southern bank afloat, the government is leading a massive 2.28 trillion recapitalisation as well as setting up a rump company to take over much of its bad loans.
With numerous public Italian banks run more as political fiefdoms than profitable organisations, no-one knows for sure if there is more bad news lurking in the system.
"Italian bank results are late, confusing and frequently restated...I hope there are no more Banco di Napolis out there but you just can't be sure," Crossley said.
Weighed down by the disastrous performance by Banco di Napoli, the Italian banking sector as a whole offered investors a feeble return on equity (ROE) of just 2.15 percent last year.
By contrast the British banking sector offered clients a ROE of around 20 percent. Even a top Italian credit institute like IMI only just managed a double digit ROE.

Italian banking heads are battling to boost profitability, but say they are not entirely to blame for the current situation, arguing that Italy's tough fiscal regime and the overcrowded nature of the sector weigh heavily.

"You have to take into account the great fragmentation of our system where weak national banks work alongside strong regional banks. In Britain just four banks work the market and they make money," said Lucio Rondelli, head of Credito Italiano.
However, despite tempting fiscal incentives for mergers, Italian banks have largely shunned calls for consolidation, with the number of banks falling just 4.5 percent between 1989-95.
The pace of mergers and acquisitions shows little sign of gathering momentum, although some consolidation is expected.
CONSOLIDATION EXPECTED

The government has pledged to sell off Banco di Napoli before the end of the year, with a number of groups, including the respected Banco Ambrosiano Veneto and BCI both interested in the cheap deposit base the southern bank offers.

Elsewhere, some analysts expect France's debt-laden Credit Lyonnais to sell control of the profitable Credito Bergamasco, while rumours abound that Popolare di Novara and Monte dei Paschi di Siena are thinking about linking up.

"Much of the best quality banking stock in Italy is to be found in these small, northern regional companies, which have a strong, loyal client base," said a Milan analyst. "What is lacking is a strong national network of banks."
What has also been lacking in numerous cases is good management, with banks building up huge amounts of bad debt in an ill-advised lending spree in the early 1990s.
Latest data from the Italian Banking Association (ABI) says bad or non-performing loans totalled 113.08 trillion lire in April, up 14.44 percent on the same month last year.
The good news for Italian banks is that recent prodigious growth in bad loans finally seems to be tailing off.
In addition, gains earlier this year on the domestic bond market coupled with handsome interest margins should help produce solid first half 1996 results.
The bad news is that the bond market has now stalled and key interest margins, the corner stone of many a balance sheet, are starting to be squeezed.
Latest Bank of Italy data for July said the average interest rate offered on client deposits was 6.57 percent against average charges for loans pegged at 12.11 percent.

The Bank of Italy lowered its discount rate in July but the Treasury has accused banks of being slow in responding and industrialists argue that the high interest charges are smothering businesses, especially in the depressed south.
ABI PREDICTS MARGINS WILL FALL

However ABI has predicted that margins will fall -- an unwelcome development for bank management at a time when they are also having to wrestle with a hike in tax on certificates of deposit, which is expected to drive clients to government bonds.

"Italian banks have to offer more services to draw in more clients, but they are also going to have to cut overheads and reduce ridiculous staffing levels," said a Milan-based banking analyst who declined to be named.
"Without rationalisation, they are not going anywhere."
